title: More Choices (If/Elif/Else)
story: A traffic light has three states: red means stop, yellow means slow down, green means go. You need more than just two choices — you need three! With `elif`, your program can handle as many possibilities as you need.
why: Real-world decisions rarely have just two options. Test scores are A, B, C, D, or F. Weather is sunny, cloudy, rainy, or snowy. `elif` lets your program handle every possibility cleanly, without piling up confusing layers of if-inside-if.
analogy: If/elif/else is like choosing your path at a multi-way intersection — each sign (condition) points you in a different direction, and you follow the first one that matches.
try_it: Give yourself different scores — 95, 82, 71, 60, 45 — and see your grade change. Then write your own elif chain for a different topic: movie ratings (G, PG, PG-13, R), or clothing sizes based on a number.
tips: Always order your `elif` conditions from highest to lowest (or lowest to highest) — never mix directions.
You can have as many `elif` blocks as you need: 3, 5, even 10 — though if you need more than 5, there might be a simpler way.
The final `else` is optional — if there's no sensible default, you can leave it out.
Variables created inside an `if`/`elif`/`else` block only exist inside that block — they disappear when the block ends.
common_mistakes: Writing `else if` instead of `elif` — XIOM uses `elif`, which is shorter and prevents a common bug called the 'dangling else' problem.
Ordering conditions randomly: `if score >= 60` before `elif score >= 90` means the `>= 90` check never runs.
Forgetting that only the FIRST matching block runs — even if later conditions would also be true.
Putting conditions after `else`: `else` is the catch-all and doesn't take a condition — `else score < 60 {` is wrong.
